title: Warm pools, Spot and the sweeper
bridge: A warm pool is like keeping a few laptops set up and asleep in a cupboard. Opening one takes a minute, not an afternoon. Except a laptop that served one run is never put back. It is destroyed, and a fresh one is set up and put to sleep in its place.
intro: A fresh VM from the image still needs minutes to boot and warm up FCP Lab. This lesson keeps a few stopped VMs ready per size, so a run gets one in about a minute. It adds cheaper Spot groups for routines that can retry. Then it adds the sweeper, which destroys anything no live run owns.

picture.caption: VMs are set up once, stopped, claimed by one run, detached, and later destroyed. The sweeper catches whatever the normal path missed.

the VM stops and waits in the pool, costing only its disk
a run raises desired by 1; a pool VM starts and is InService in about a minute

warm VM older than 24 h: recycle, so the pool tracks the newest image

p: An Auto Scaling group (ASG) keeps a number of VMs from a launch template. You set the desired count, and it starts or stops VMs to match. A warm pool is a set of VMs the group has already booted and set up, then stopped. When the group needs one more VM, it starts a stopped one instead of building a new one.

A stopped VM costs only its disk, about $8 to $10 a month. A full VM costs about $0.42 an hour while it runs. So a few warm VMs per size are cheap, and they turn a cold start of many minutes into about one minute.

G3-15 makes one ASG per size. The steady state is all-warm: desired 0, nothing in service until a run claims a VM. The pools start at lite 2, full 2, wide 0. max_size is 3, because only claims in flight live in the group.

sections.h: The ASG, part 1: the group and its pool
p: The group sits in the sandbox subnets and uses the size's launch template from lesson g3-6. The warm_pool block says how many stopped VMs to keep.
sections.because: We set reuse_on_scale_in = false, because a VM that served a run holds that run's files and must never serve another one.

notes.text: One group per size, like the launch templates.
The three private sandbox subnets, one per availability zone.
At most 3 VMs in service: only claims in flight. A claimed VM is detached at once, so it no longer counts.
Desired 0: nothing runs until a claim raises it.
$Latest: the group always launches from the newest version of the template.
Pool VMs are stopped, not running. Only the disk is billed.
How many to keep, per size: lite 2, full 2, wide 0 to start.
Cap the pool at the same number, so it never grows on its own.
A VM leaving service is terminated, never returned to the pool.

callout.text: One fresh VM per run. A claimed VM is detached from its group, used by one run, and destroyed. Nothing goes back to the pool.

sections.h: The ASG, part 2: finish setup before stopping
p: A VM that joins the warm pool should do its slow first-boot work before it stops. It starts FCP Lab once, pulls images and reads the disk. A lifecycle hook pauses the VM at a point in its life until something says 'continue'.

The other half is a systemd unit in the image role, sandbox-warm. On boot it reads /latest/meta-data/autoscaling/target-lifecycle-state from the metadata service. Warmed:Stopped means 'going to the pool': start FCP Lab once, stop it, complete the hook. InService means a run is waiting: complete the hook at once.
sections.because: We hold every new VM at launch until it reports ready, because a half-set-up warm VM breaks the next run.

notes.text: What the hook waits for: FCP Lab started once, images pulled, disk warmed.
The hook fires when a VM launches, for the warm pool or straight into service.
The VM has 1800 seconds (30 minutes) to complete the hook.
If it never does, ABANDON: the group terminates that VM and tries a new one.
Tags on the group copy to each VM: the account's tags, ai-agents:managed=true and the size.

p: The claim activity (lesson g3-8) raises desired by 1. The group starts a warm VM and waits for its hook. When the VM is InService, the activity calls DetachInstances with ShouldDecrementDesiredCapacity. The VM leaves the group, and desired goes back down.

From then on Temporal owns the VM, not the group. The group sees its pool is one short and boots a replacement, which goes through the hook and stops. The completed hook is why the instance role has autoscaling:CompleteLifecycleAction, and why the VPC has an autoscaling endpoint (lesson g3-2).

There is one more cap above all of this. The account's On-Demand and Spot vCPU quotas limit how many VMs can run at once. Check them and request what we need; runs above the cap wait in Temporal's slot queues (G3-25).

Spot VMs are spare EC2 capacity sold about 56% cheaper. AWS can take one back with a two-minute warning. A routine that can retry, such as a CI fixer, does not mind. spot-watch writes /run/nova/preempt and the harness saves its work. Then the workflow retries the step on a fresh VM (lesson g3-8).

Nova and the bug fixers stay on the on-demand groups. They wait on people, and a lost VM costs a person's time. Spot groups have no warm pool. lite and full each get one, named ai-agents-sandbox-<size>-spot.
sections.because: We let the group pick among three instance families, because Spot capacity runs out per type.

notes.text: lite and full only. wide has no Spot group.
The name acquireSandbox builds when spot is true: ai-agents-sandbox-full-spot.
A mixed instances policy lets one group use several instance types and buying options.
0% on-demand above the base: every VM in this group is Spot.
price-capacity-optimized picks the cheapest Spot pools that are least likely to be taken back.
The same launch template as the on-demand group: same image, role and walls.
One override per family: m8i, m7i and m6i of the same size, for example m7i.2xlarge.

p: Throw-away machines must really be thrown away, even when the orchestrator is down or a run crashed. G3-22 adds a Lambda in the ai-agents account that runs every 15 minutes and works only from tags. It does not ask Temporal anything, so it keeps working when Temporal does not.

It is a copy of modules/aws-vm-autostop: an EventBridge rule rate(15 minutes), a Python Lambda and tag-scoped IAM. It stays Python although the platform is TypeScript: the infrastructure repo builds its Lambdas in Python with uv, and DevOps owns them. It is not attached to the VPC, so it needs no endpoints.
sections.because: We decide from tags alone, because the cleaner must not depend on the system whose failures it cleans up after.

notes.text: boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python, the Python twin of the SDK v3 clients in TypeScript.
Dry by default: it only logs what it would do, until DevOps sets DRY_RUN=false.
One 'now' for the whole run, in UTC.
Only instances tagged ai-agents:managed=true. Nothing else in the account is touched.
Turn AWS's tag list into a dict, so tags["ai-agents:run-id"] works.
A claimed VM has a run-id. If its lease time has passed, no live run renewed it, so nobody owns it.
Stopped for over 72 hours. A parked VM is retired by its workflow at 72 h; this rule is the backstop.
A warm VM (still in a group) launched over 24 hours ago is recycled, so the pool refills from the newest image.
Available volumes are attached to nothing. A managed one is an orphaned disk.

sections.h: The sweeper, part 2: act, but dry first
p: Every decision goes through act. It always prints one JSON line, so a dry run shows exactly what a real run would do. The IAM role allows ec2:TerminateInstances and ec2:DeleteVolume only when aws:ResourceTag/ai-agents:managed is true, and autoscaling:TerminateInstanceInAutoScalingGroup on the sandbox ASGs only.
sections.because: We start with dry_run = true, because a cleaner with a wrong rule destroys the wrong things every 15 minutes.

notes.text: One JSON line per action: what, which id, why, and whether it was dry. CloudWatch Logs keeps it.
Dry: stop after logging.
terminate: an orphan whose lease passed, or a VM stopped too long.
recycle: terminate inside the group without lowering desired, so the group launches a new VM from the current image.
The only other action: delete an orphaned volume.

callout.text: The Lambda also publishes CloudWatch metrics in AIAgents/Sweeper (OrphansTerminated, VolumesDeleted) for G3-34's alerts. Ask DevOps where the CloudWatch exporter config lives, and add the namespace there.

lab.faded: Add spot.tf with the Spot groups from section 5. Plan: expect 13 to add. The last step is yours. List the override instance types with one grep on the plan. Say why you see six lines, not nine.
lab.alone: Write the sweeper's IAM rule as a data "aws_iam_policy_document" "sweeper" in sweeper_iam.tf. Allow ec2:TerminateInstances and ec2:DeleteVolume on * with a condition: StringEquals on aws:ResourceTag/ai-agents:managed = "true". Add output "sweeper_policy" { value = data.aws_iam_policy_document.sweeper.json }. Run the plan and find the StringEquals block in the output. Then say what the policy would allow if you forgot the condition.
lab.done: The plan shows three groups with Stopped pools of 2, 2 and 0 and the ABANDON hook. It also shows two Spot groups and a tag-conditioned sweeper policy.

quiz.q: A full VM finished run-42. Its group has reuse_on_scale_in = false. What happens to that VM?

options.text: It is stopped and returned to the warm pool for the next run.
options.why: It was detached when it was claimed, and a used VM never goes back. It holds run-42's files.

options.text: releaseSandbox terminates it; the group already refilled its pool when the VM was detached.
options.why: One fresh VM per run. The pool refills from the image, never from used VMs.

options.text: The sweeper keeps it 24 hours in case run-42 is resumed.
options.why: A resume uses a fresh VM and the session store. Nothing waits for a finished run.

quiz.q: Why do Nova and the bug fixers use on-demand groups instead of Spot?

options.why: They are ordinary EC2 VMs from the same launch template.

options.text: Spot is not allowed in the ai-agents account.
options.why: Routines use Spot groups in the same account.

options.text: They wait on people, so a VM taken back by AWS costs a person's time, not only a retry.
options.why: Spot fits work that can retry on its own. A run waiting for an answer is not that.

quiz.q: The orchestrator was down for a day. A parked VM has been stopped for 80 hours. What does the sweeper do?

options.text: Terminates it: stopped for over 72 h. Its work was saved at every checkpoint, and the next answer resumes on a fresh VM.
options.why: The 72-hour rule is the backstop for retireSandbox, and it needs nothing from Temporal.

options.text: Nothing, because its lease (now + 73 h when parked) has not expired.
options.why: The rules are checked in order. The lease rule does not match, but the stopped-over-72-h rule does.

options.text: Starts it and runs nova-worker checkpoint first.
options.why: That is what retireSandbox does in the workflow. The sweeper only terminates and deletes.

words.plain: An AWS group that keeps a desired number of VMs from a launch template.
VMs a group has booted, set up and stopped, ready to start in about a minute.
A pause in a VM's launch until something completes it, or a timeout decides.
Take a VM out of its group, so the group no longer counts or replaces it.
Spare EC2 capacity, about 56% cheaper, that AWS can take back with two minutes' warning.
ai-agents:lease-until on a claimed VM; a live run renews it, and the sweeper ends VMs whose lease passed.

tickets.why: This lesson explained the warm-pool groups line by line, the setup hook, detaching on claim, and the Spot groups.
walk: In modules/aws-sandbox-pool add asg.tf (code above): one group per size, desired 0, min 0, max 3, plus the tag blocks.
Set warm_pool from var.warm_pool_size (lite 2, full 2, wide 0) with pool_state Stopped and reuse_on_scale_in = false.
Add the initial_lifecycle_hook (EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING, 1800 s, ABANDON). Add the sandbox-warm systemd unit to the image role: Warmed:Stopped warms FCP Lab first; InService completes at once.
Hand G3-18 the claim rule: raise desired by 1, wait for InService, DetachInstances with ShouldDecrementDesiredCapacity.
Add Spot groups for lite and full: 0% on-demand, price-capacity-optimized, overrides m8i, m7i and m6i of the same size, no warm pool.
Check the account's On-Demand and Spot vCPU quotas and request what we need.

tickets.why: This lesson explained the four sweeper rules and act() line by line, the tag-scoped IAM and the dry-run start.
walk: Copy modules/aws-vm-autostop to modules/aws-sandbox-sweeper (EventBridge rate(15 minutes), Python Lambda built with uv), not attached to the VPC. Add the unit terraform/accounts/ai-agents/aws/us-east-1/sandboxes/sweeper/.
Write lambda/handler.py (code above) with managed_instances, managed_volumes, parse and stopped_since helpers.
IAM: ec2:TerminateInstances and ec2:DeleteVolume only with aws:ResourceTag/ai-agents:managed = true; autoscaling:TerminateInstanceInAutoScalingGroup on the sandbox ASGs only.
Start with DRY_RUN=true, read the JSON lines for a while, then switch it off in a PR a person approves.
Publish CloudWatch metrics AIAgents/Sweeper (OrphansTerminated, VolumesDeleted) and add the namespace to the CloudWatch exporter with DevOps.
Set the On-Demand and Spot vCPU quotas as the final cap; above it, runs wait in the Temporal slot queues (G3-25).

remember: A VM is set up once, claimed by one run, then destroyed; the sweeper catches what that path missed.
